title: The Night the Lights Went Out
setting: a regional hospital's IT night shift

post.author: u/ulverby_sitemanager_yewande
post.title: I run a hospital overnight. Last night our disaster plan met its target, and the report says so. The lab's blood results sat where no doctor could see them until 08:40.

blocks.text: I'm Yewande, a senior nurse. At night I'm the site manager: the one person in charge of all of Ulverby General until morning. In a crisis that makes me the incident commander, who decides and keeps the timeline. I'm not IT.

At 01:20 a fault hit our substation, the fenced yard where the city's power enters the hospital. The lights went out for a breath. Then our generators, the hospital's own diesel engines, took over the wards and computers. Not the cooling in the locked room where the computers live.

That room is the data room, where the hospital's systems run. A system is one program with its own stored records: lab results, medicines, payroll. Without cooling the room heated fast. At 01:30 Chibuzo, who leads the IT night shift, shut it down before the heat broke anything.

Then he opened the disaster recovery plan: how to bring our systems back somewhere else. Ours is the second site, a spare data room at our sister hospital in Selsby, 30 km away. Every night at 01:00 it gets a fresh copy of each system; last night's finished at 01:12. The pharmacy's copy runs at 20:00, when its counter closes.

Restoring a system takes three steps: start it at the second site, load its last copy, check it. Our supplier, Draycott, wrote the plan three years ago: one system at a time, smallest first, about an hour each. It sets one target for all, its RTO, short for recovery time objective: everything back within 8 hours of the fault. That made 09:20.
Nobody had ever used it, not even as a practice. Our monthly generator test never touches the cooling; it sits on its own supply, and that supply isn't on the plan's list.

The first restore started at 01:40. Seven systems, smallest first: the staff directory, payroll, email, theatre lists (who has an operation in the morning), pharmacy (every patient's medicines and doses), admissions (who is in which bed), and lab results, the largest. It went last.

All night the lab's machines kept testing blood. No doctor could see the results on a screen. By 02:00 the emergency department was sending porters to carry paper. The wards upstairs waited. Payroll was back by 03:30.
This morning Draycott's tool printed the recovery report. Each line shows one system, when its restore started and ended, and whether it met the 8-hour target.

system           start  end    target met
staff directory  01:40  02:30  yes
payroll          02:30  03:30  yes
email            03:30  04:30  yes
theatre lists    04:30  05:30  yes
pharmacy         05:30  06:30  yes
admissions       06:30  07:30  yes
lab results      07:30  08:40  yes
08:40 all systems restored within target

diagram.aria: 01:00 to 09:20. The fault comes at 01:20 and every system is down from 01:30. Restores run one at a time from 01:40: staff directory 01:40 to 02:30, payroll 02:30 to 03:30, email 03:30 to 04:30, theatre lists 04:30 to 05:30, pharmacy 05:30 to 06:30, admissions 06:30 to 07:30, lab results 07:30 to 08:40. The report's line comes at 08:40; the 8-hour target is 09:20.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the recovery report. One restore at a time, smallest first. Payroll was back at 03:30. The lab's results were unseen on screens from 01:30 to 08:40, and the report's last line still says all within target.

blocks.text: Pharmacy came back at 06:30 from its 20:00 copy. How much recent work you lose, from the last copy to the stop, is the RPO, short for recovery point objective. The pharmacy's was five and a half hours. Marjatta, our night pharmacist, found 46 dose changes missing, and checked each against the wards' paper drug charts, bed by bed.
All systems restored within target. Every line of the report is true.
Draycott wants to sign the plan off as tested. Before I sign too: what should we change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: The plan did exactly what it says, and the report is honest about what it measured. When the Building Burns has more on RTO and RPO; for now, look at the report's first column instead. It lists systems. Your wards don't feel systems; they feel processes. A process is one piece of the hospital's work: a blood result reaching a doctor, a dose reaching a patient, staff being paid. Each process has a deadline, the longest it can stop before people are hurt. Who did Draycott ask about deadlines?

replies.author: u/ulverby_sitemanager_yewande
replies.text: Nobody on the wards, as far as I can find. Draycott asked IT for the size of each system. And this morning their account manager emailed: "If 8 hours is too slow for you, we can write 1 hour for every system."

replies.author: u/grey_pager
replies.text: Asking every department for its deadline, and writing the answers down, is called a business impact analysis, a BIA for short. Your plan was written from sizes. Read the report again with the wards' deadlines beside it.

comments.author: u/volts_first_ferreira
comments.text: Respectfully, you're all tidying the queue for a disaster you could have stopped. The real failure was the substation; spend the money on power, not paperwork. A bigger generator that carries the cooling too, and a second cooling unit beside the first. A data room that never goes down never needs a restore order. Every hour spent on plans is an hour not spent on the thing that actually broke.

comments.author: u/ulverby_it_chibuzo
comments.text: Chibuzo here, IT night lead. I followed the plan line by line, and I'd change one thing. Next time I start every restore at Selsby at once. The link, the line our copies travel along to Selsby, is fast, the spare room has space, and there are two of us on nights. Then nothing waits its turn last, and the lab isn't stuck behind payroll.

reply.prompt: Draycott wants the plan signed off as tested. What should Ulverby General change before the next night like this? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Fit a bigger generator and a second cooling unit, so the data room never goes down.
options.part2: Draycott fitted a bigger generator that carries the cooling, and a second cooling unit, by spring. In the sim I switched both on and replayed last night: the substation fault comes at 01:20 and the room stays up, with nothing to restore. Then I chose the next thing on our risk list, a pipe bursting over the data room at the same minute. Chibuzo shut the room at 01:30 again, and the same plan ran in the same order: payroll back at 03:30, pharmacy at 06:30, lab results at 08:40, and the report said all systems restored within target. Three processes past their deadlines, 10 h 40 min in all. Ferreira's money bought a safer room, and the same night in every other way.
options.senior: Prevention lowers how often a disaster comes; continuity decides what happens when one comes anyway. Both matter, and the generator is worth fitting, but no room is safe from every cause: water, fire, a failed disk store, ransomware. Business continuity starts from the room being gone, whatever the cause, and asks which work must come back first. A fix aimed at last night's cause leaves the order, the deadlines and the pharmacy's 20:00 copy exactly as they were.

options.text: Restore every system at once at the second site, so nothing has to wait its turn last.
options.part2: We tried Chibuzo's way in the sim first. At 01:40 all seven restores start together and share the link to Selsby and the two engineers equally, so each runs at a seventh of the speed. The staff directory, the smallest, is back at 07:30. Payroll, email, theatre lists, pharmacy and admissions all come back together at 08:30. Lab results at 08:40, the same minute as last night. Payroll moved from 03:30 to 08:30, and the lab gained nothing. Time past deadlines: 14 h 50 min, against 10 h 40 min last night; the theatre lists missed theirs too. The link carries the same copies whether they come in a line or all at once.
options.senior: Restoring in parallel only helps when there is spare capacity: a link, disks and people sitting idle while one restore runs. Last night the link and the two engineers were the limit, so splitting them seven ways made every restore seven times slower and pushed every finish towards the end. The total work doesn't shrink; what you choose is who gets the capacity first. Parallel restores suit independent systems on separate links and teams. With one shared pipe, order beats parallel.

options.text: Set a one-hour target for every system, so even the last one is back within the hour.
options.part2: Draycott wrote 1 hour for every system and priced how to meet it: a standby copy of all seven, kept running at Selsby and updated all day, ready to take over. The board turned the price down, so the 1-hour targets stayed on paper over the same plan. In the sim, last night with a 1-hour target for all: the same order, payroll at 03:30, lab results at 08:40, and the report now says 0 of 7 restored within target. The report got honest. The lab waited exactly as long.
options.senior: A target is a promise, not a mechanism. One hour for everything means a standby copy of everything, including payroll, which can wait three days, so most of the money buys speed nobody needs. And a target on its own says nothing about order: one restore at a time can't meet seven 1-hour targets. Set each process's target from its deadline, pay for standby only where the deadline is shorter than a restore (here, perhaps the lab), and let the rest wait their turn. That is the trade: money for minutes, spent where minutes hurt.

options.text: Order recovery by each process's deadline: lab results first, and payroll later.
options.part2: We asked every department for its deadline. Lab results: 1 hour. Pharmacy: 3 hours. Admissions: 4. Theatre lists: 6, before the first operation. Email: a day. The directory and payroll: 3 days. Chibuzo rewrote the order by those deadlines, and each department wrote its paper routine for the gap into the runbook beside the plan. In the sim, last night replayed: lab results back at 02:50, pharmacy 03:50, admissions 04:50, theatre lists 05:50, email 06:50, the directory 07:40, payroll 08:40. The report reads the same, all systems restored within target at 08:40. On the wards, one deadline missed, the lab's by 30 minutes, and the lab's paper round covers it. Time past deadlines: 30 minutes, against 10 h 40 min.
options.senior: Recover the work, not the machines. A business impact analysis asks each process how fast it hurts when it stops, and that deadline sets its RTO and its place in the order: shortest deadline first, whatever its size. The same seven hours of restoring now ends with payroll instead of the lab. Where no restore can beat a deadline (the lab's takes 70 minutes against 1 hour), a manual workaround in the runbook covers the gap, or you pay for standby for that one system. Set each process's RPO the same way: the pharmacy can't lose five and a half hours of dose changes. Then rehearse it, because a plan nobody has run is a guess.

sim.title: Run the recovery from 01:10 to 09:00
sim.lede: You're Yewande at 01:10, before the fault. At 01:20 the substation fault stops the data room's cooling; at 01:30 Chibuzo shuts the room down. From 01:40 the second site at Selsby restores seven systems from their last copies. Each restore takes its time from the plan's table: 50 minutes for the directory, 70 for lab results, 60 for each of the others. A restore running alone gets the whole link and both engineers; restores running together share them equally. Each process has a deadline from the business impact analysis, counted from 01:20: lab results 1 hour, pharmacy 3, admissions 4, theatre lists 6, email 24, the directory and payroll 72. The pharmacy's copy is from 20:00, the others' from 01:00. Each step is 10 minutes. Choose the order, the targets the report uses, the runbook workarounds, the pharmacy's copy schedule, the cause and the new generator. Or turn on tabletop mode: a rehearsal at a table, where timed messages called injects arrive as posts, the run stops, and you make the call.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run to 03:30: payroll is back and lab results haven't started. Run to 09:00: lab results at 08:40, the report says all systems restored within target, 3 of 7 deadlines missed, 10 h 40 min past deadlines, 46 doses missing. Order by process deadline and run again: lab results at 02:50, payroll at 08:40, 30 min past deadlines. All at once: payroll at 08:30, lab results still 08:40, 14 h 50 min. A 1-hour target for every system: the report says 0 of 7. The new generator: no restore at all; then pick the burst pipe: lab results at 08:40 again. Copy the pharmacy every 15 minutes: 1 dose missing. Then turn on tabletop mode and answer the four injects.

explain.oneLine: Nothing failed. The plan restored seven systems one at a time, smallest first, and met its single 8-hour target at 08:40. Nobody had asked which work hurts first: lab results needed to be back within 1 hour and came last, while payroll could wait 3 days and came second. Order recovery by each process's deadline, cover the gaps with written workarounds, and rehearse it.

steps.title: One target, measured on systems.
steps.text: Draycott's plan had one RTO, the recovery time objective: every system back within 8 hours of the fault, so by 09:20. The report checks each system against that one number, and each one passed: the last, lab results, at 08:40. But a hospital doesn't run systems; it runs processes, pieces of work such as getting a blood result to a doctor. The report measured the machines, and the harm was in the work. Every line of it was true, and none of its lines could show that the most urgent work waited longest.

steps.title: Smallest first is an order nobody chose.
steps.text: Each restore runs in steps. First, the system is started at the second site in Selsby. Second, its last copy is loaded over the link; a large copy takes longer, and this is where size bites. Third, an engineer checks it before the wards are told to use it; a missed check means wards trust a broken system. Draycott's plan queued the seven by size, smallest first, a common supplier default because small restores finish early and the progress bar moves. Size has nothing to do with harm. The lab system is the largest, so the order put the most urgent work last, and payroll, which can wait three days, second.

steps.title: A business impact analysis finds the deadlines.
steps.text: It works in steps. First, list the processes: lab results, medicines, beds, operations, pay. Second, ask each department how the harm grows while its process is stopped, hour by hour. Third, find the point where that harm becomes unacceptable: that is the process's deadline, and it becomes its RTO. Fourth, list what each process needs to run: systems, people, suppliers and other processes. ISO 22301 puts this in clause 8.2.2. At Ulverby the answers are 1 hour for lab results, 3 for pharmacy, 4 for admissions, 6 for theatre lists, a day for email and 3 days for the directory and payroll. Restore in that order and the same seven hours end with payroll, not the lab: one deadline missed by 30 minutes instead of three by 10 h 40 min in all.

steps.title: RPO per process: the pharmacy's 20:00 copy.
steps.text: The RPO, recovery point objective, is how much recent work you can lose: the time from the last good copy to the moment things stop. Every system got the same nightly copy at 01:00, except the pharmacy's, set at 20:00 three years ago when its counter closed. So the pharmacy came back without anything changed between 20:00 and 01:30: 46 dose changes. A medicines process needs its copy taken often, every few minutes; payroll is fine with once a day. Decide the RPO per process from the impact analysis, then set each system's copy schedule to meet it. In the sim, copies every 15 minutes leave 1 change missing instead of 46.

steps.title: Workarounds, words and rehearsal.
steps.text: Even the best order leaves gaps: no restore of 70 minutes beats a 1-hour deadline. A runbook, the written step-by-step for each process, holds its manual workaround for that gap: the lab prints results and porters run them to every ward on a round, with urgent ones phoned. Crisis communication is part of the plan too: who tells the wards (the site manager), who tells families (the switchboard, from an agreed script), who tells the public (the communications lead). One incident commander decides and keeps the timeline, as in The Pager. Then rehearse: a tabletop exercise puts the people around a table, a facilitator plays the night out as messages called injects, and the gaps show up on paper instead of on the wards.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the next bad night. A business impact analysis sets each process's deadline; the deadlines sort the recovery order; the order drives restores at the second site, lab results first. Below, the incident commander starts the runbook workarounds and gives each restore its go.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next bad night. The impact analysis gives each process a deadline, the deadlines sort the recovery order, and the second site restores lab results first, back at 02:50. The runbook's paper round covers the lab's last 30 minutes, and one incident commander starts it and gives each restore its go.

fix.title: The fix: deadlines first, then the order, then a rehearsal
fix.text: Run a business impact analysis: ask every department how fast harm grows when its process stops, and write down each deadline. Set each process's RTO from its deadline and each RPO from how much work it can lose. Re-order the plan by deadline, shortest first: lab results, pharmacy, admissions, theatre lists, email, the directory, payroll. Copy the pharmacy every 15 minutes, not once a day at 20:00. Write each department's manual workaround into the runbook, with who starts it. Write the crisis words: the site manager tells the wards, the switchboard tells families from a script, the communications lead tells the public. Then run a tabletop exercise before signing anything. In the sim, the deadline order gives lab results at 02:50 and 30 minutes past deadlines instead of 10 h 40 min, with the same report line at 08:40.

limits: The order can't beat physics. The lab's restore takes 70 minutes, so even first it misses its 1-hour deadline by 30 minutes. Only a workaround or a standby copy closes that gap, and a standby copy costs money every day.
Deadlines change. A new ward, a new contract or a process that moves onto a system makes last year's impact analysis wrong. It needs re-asking at least yearly and after every big change.

Processes depend on each other. A result is filed against a patient's record, so restoring one system first may be useless until another is back. The analysis must list what each process needs, not only how fast it hurts.

explain.seniorTake: Business continuity is about the work, not the machines. A disaster recovery plan says how to bring systems back; a continuity plan says which work must come back first, how to keep going on paper until it does, and who says what to whom meanwhile. The order comes from a business impact analysis: for each process, how fast the harm grows and the point where it becomes unacceptable. That point is its deadline, and it sets the RTO; how much work it can lose sets its RPO. One target for all hides the order, so measure each process against its own deadline and report that, not the systems. Spend money where a deadline is shorter than any restore, and let the rest wait their turn. And rehearse: a plan that has never been run is a guess with a signature on it. A tabletop exercise, with injects that arrive at their times and people who must make the calls, finds the missing order, the missing script and the missing workaround on a quiet afternoon instead of at 01:30.

realWorld.title: ISO 22301:2019, clause 8.2.2: business impact analysis
realWorld.text: Cyberday's summary of the clause: the organization must identify critical activities and "evaluate the escalating consequences of their disruption over time against defined criteria", determine "the point at which impacts become unacceptable", and so set "recovery time objectives for resuming operations at a minimum capacity", identifying the resources and dependencies these activities need. This is a summary, not the standard's own text.

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-84 (2006): what a tabletop exercise is
realWorld.text: "Tabletop exercises are discussion-based exercises where personnel meet in a classroom setting or in breakout groups to discuss their roles during an emergency and their responses to a particular emergency situation. A facilitator presents a scenario and asks the exercise participants questions related to the scenario." It adds: "A tabletop exercise is discussion-based only and does not involve deploying equipment or other resources."

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-84: injects, from its functional exercise samples
realWorld.text: The guide's functional exercise samples use timed messages called injects. Its sample inject is "The vehicle transporting the backup tapes to the restoration site is in a traffic jam, and is expected to arrive 3 hours later than originally scheduled." It says message injects "can be provided in many forms, including e-mails, letters, memoranda, telephone calls, and radio call scripts." The sim's tabletop mode borrows that idea; the guide itself describes tabletops as discussion around a scenario.

realWorld.title: NIST glossary: the tabletop's purpose
realWorld.text: NIST's glossary, citing SP 800-84, says participants meet "to validate the content of the plan by discussing their roles during an emergency", and "A facilitator initiates the discussion by presenting a scenario and asking questions based on the scenario."

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.5.30: an RTO for each service
realWorld.text: ISMS.online's summary of control A.5.30, ICT readiness for business continuity, says "a thorough BIA must be conducted" and that the plan should include "A clear RTO for each ICT service in question and how the organisation intends to restore them", with a recovery point objective defined "For each ICT resource". Control A.5.29 is information security during disruption.

realWorld.title: SOC 2 A1.3: test the recovery plan
realWorld.text: The availability criterion A1.3 reads: "The entity tests recovery plan procedures supporting system recovery to meet its objectives." Ulverby's plan sat three years without a test, which is the gap this criterion looks for.

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, for running the whole program
realWorld.text: NIST's Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems (2010) covers the whole planning cycle, with a business impact analysis template. Running a continuity program year after year is The Drill's subject, later in the course.

asked: What is a business impact analysis?
How do you decide recovery order?
How would you run a tabletop exercise?
interview.answer: A business impact analysis asks, for each business process, not each system, how the harm grows while it is stopped and when it becomes unacceptable. That point is the process's deadline, and it sets its RTO, the recovery time objective. The same analysis sets the RPO, the recovery point objective: how much recent work the process can lose, which decides how often its data must be copied. It also lists what each process depends on: systems, people, suppliers and other processes. Recovery order then follows the deadlines, shortest first, with dependencies pulled forward, whatever the systems' sizes. Where no restore can beat a deadline, you either pay for a standby copy of that one system or write a manual workaround into the runbook and start it at once. To run a tabletop exercise: pick a realistic scenario, gather the people who would really be on the night, appoint a facilitator, and prepare a list of injects, timed messages such as "the lab system is still down at 02:20" or "a reporter is on the phone". Play the night out loud at the table: each inject arrives, the room decides, the facilitator notes what the plan did not answer. Finish with a short report of the gaps and who fixes each. NIST SP 800-84 describes tabletops this way: discussion only, around a scenario, with a facilitator asking questions. A story I'd tell: a hospital's plan restored seven systems smallest first under one 8-hour target. It met the target at 08:40, and lab results, needed within an hour, came last. Ordered by deadline, the lab was back at 02:50, payroll last, and the report read the same.

terms.def: The regional hospital in this story. Its systems run in one data room on site, with a second site at its sister hospital in Selsby.
The senior nurse in charge of the whole hospital overnight. Yewande's job; in a crisis she is the incident commander.
The one person in charge of an incident: they decide, give each change its go, and keep the timeline. Taught in The Pager.
The fenced yard where the city's power comes into the hospital and is stepped down for its buildings. Last night's fault was there.
The hospital's own diesel engines that make power when the city's supply fails. Ulverby's carried the wards and computers, not the data room's cooling.
The locked, chilled room where the hospital's systems run. Without cooling it heats up within minutes, so it had to be shut down at 01:30.
The air-conditioning machine that keeps a data room cool. Ulverby's runs on its own supply, which the generator does not feed.
One program with its own stored records, such as the lab results system or payroll. Ulverby's plan restores seven of them.
One piece of the hospital's work, such as a blood result reaching a doctor or staff being paid. A process may use several systems.
The written plan for bringing systems back somewhere else after losing a whole site. Ulverby's was written by Draycott three years ago.
A spare data room somewhere else that receives copies of each system and can run them. Ulverby's is at its sister hospital in Selsby, 30 km away.
A saved copy of a system's data, kept so it can be put back. Ulverby's are sent to Selsby nightly at 01:00, the pharmacy's at 20:00.
Bringing a system back from its copy, in steps: start it at the second site, load the last copy, check it. Work after the copy is missing.
The line that carries data between the hospital and the second site. Restores running at once share it.
The company that sells and supports a system or a service. Draycott is Ulverby's recovery supplier.
The fictional supplier that wrote Ulverby's recovery plan and runs its restore tool.
The time a plan promises to be back by. Ulverby's plan had one for every system: 8 hours from the fault, so 09:20.
Short for recovery time objective: how long something may stay down. Best set per process from its deadline, not once for every system.
Short for recovery point objective: how much recent work you can afford to lose, from the last good copy to the disaster. The pharmacy's real one was 5 h 30 min.
The longest a process can stop before people are hurt: 1 hour for lab results, 3 days for payroll. It sets the process's RTO.
Asking every department how fast harm grows when its process stops, finding each deadline and what each process needs, and writing it down.
Short for business impact analysis.
The sequence in which systems are restored. Draycott's default was smallest first; the fix is shortest deadline first.
The restore tool's summary: each system's restore start and end and whether it met its target. Ulverby's said all within target at 08:40.
Keeping the organisation's most important work going through a disaster, on systems or on paper, and bringing it back in the right order.
A way to keep a process going by hand while its system is down, such as printed lab results carried to the wards by porters.
The written step-by-step for a job or a bad night, kept where the night shift can find it. The fix puts each workaround in it.
The plan for who tells whom what in a disaster: here the site manager tells wards, the switchboard tells families, the communications lead tells the public.
A copy of a system kept running at the second site and updated all day, ready to take over in minutes. Fast, and paid for every day.
An attack that locks an organisation's data and demands payment. One of many causes that can take a data room out.
Something a process or system needs in order to work, such as another system, a supplier or a person.
A rehearsal at a table: the people who would be on the night talk through a scenario as a facilitator brings it to them. Nothing is switched off.
A timed message in an exercise, such as "the lab is still down at 02:20", that the players must respond to.
The person who runs a tabletop exercise: presents the scenario, delivers the injects and asks the questions.
A rehearsal where people carry out their duties in a simulated setting, a step beyond a tabletop. NIST SP 800-84 describes both.
The hospital's list of who has an operation, in which operating theatre, in the morning.
The system that records who is in which bed, and every patient's admission record.
A hospital worker who moves patients and things around the building. Last night they carried paper lab results to the emergency department.
The international standard for business continuity management. Its clause 8.2.2 covers business impact analysis.
An international standard for running information security. Its Annex A controls A.5.29 and A.5.30 cover security during disruption and ICT readiness for continuity.
Short for information and communication technology: computers, networks and the systems on them.
An audit report, written by an outside checker, on a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria.
A SOC 2 availability criterion: the entity tests recovery plan procedures supporting system recovery to meet its objectives.
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology. Its SP 800-84 guide covers tests, training and exercises for IT plans.

atWork: Find your recovery plan and look at the order it restores things in. It is a common pattern for a plan to restore systems in a supplier's default order, by size or alphabetically, under one target for everything, so that it meets its target while the most urgent work waits last. Check three things. Does a business impact analysis exist, naming each business process, its deadline (its RTO), how much work it can lose (its RPO) and what it depends on? Does the restore order follow those deadlines, and does each process's copy schedule meet its RPO? And has the plan ever been rehearsed, at least as a tabletop exercise with timed injects, with the people who would really be on the night? On AWS, the same questions apply to the order your runbooks rebuild services in another region. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO 22301:2019, clause 8.2.2 asks for a business impact analysis that sets prioritised time frames for resuming activities; if ISO/IEC 27001:2022, controls A.5.29 (information security during disruption) and A.5.30 (ICT readiness for business continuity) expect an RTO and RPO for each service; if SOC 2, criterion A1.3 asks you to test recovery plan procedures. NIST SP 800-84 describes how to run the tabletop. A dated impact analysis, a plan ordered by it, and a written exercise report are the evidence an auditor will ask for, so build them in now, not at audit time.

recall.prompt: An online shop's recovery plan rebuilds its five services at a backup data centre in alphabetical order, about 40 minutes each, with one goal: all back within 4 hours. In a drill it finishes in 3 h 20 min, inside the goal, but checkout, which loses sales every minute it is down, comes back fourth, after the staff wiki and the reporting tool. The operations lead says the plan passed. What do you tell her, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: One shared goal measures machines, not the work; it hides which part of the business hurts first
Run a business impact analysis to find each process's deadline, its RTO
Rebuild in deadline order: checkout first, the wiki last

recall.model: The plan passed its own test and still failed the business. One target for all four hours measures machines, not the work, and alphabetical order is an order nobody chose. Run a business impact analysis: ask each team how fast harm grows when its process stops, and write down each deadline as that process's own RTO. Checkout loses money every minute, so it has the shortest deadline; the wiki can wait a day. Reorder the rebuild by deadline, shortest deadline first: checkout first, the wiki last. If checkout's deadline is shorter than any rebuild, keep a standby copy of checkout alone, and report each process against its own deadline next time.

recall.prompt: What does a business impact analysis give you?
options: A list of every system's size, so the smallest can be restored first
Each process's deadline, how much work it can lose, and what it depends on
A single recovery target that every system must meet
A guarantee that the data room will never go down
recall.why: It asks each department how fast harm grows when its process stops. The point where it becomes unacceptable is the deadline, which sets the RTO; how much work it can lose sets the RPO; and it lists each process's dependencies. ISO 22301 clause 8.2.2 asks for it.

recall.prompt: Ulverby's pharmacy copy runs once a day at 20:00, and the data room was shut down at 01:30. What was the pharmacy's real RPO last night?
options: Nothing, because the restore finished within target
recall.why: The RPO is the work lost between the last good copy and the moment things stopped: 20:00 to 01:30, five and a half hours, which held 46 dose changes. The restore's speed has nothing to do with it.

recall.prompt: In a tabletop exercise, as NIST SP 800-84 describes it, what happens?
options: The real data room is switched off and the team restores every system
People talk through their roles in a scenario a facilitator presents, without deploying equipment
The supplier runs the restore tool alone and sends the report
Each system is tested on its own to prove its copy loads
recall.why: NIST SP 800-84: tabletop exercises are discussion-based; a facilitator presents a scenario and asks questions, and a tabletop does not involve deploying equipment or other resources. Timed injects make the night play out in order.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. We asked every department for its deadline, and the plan now restores lab results first. We rehearsed it at a table in March. On 2 August a fan in the cooling failed at 01:20, and Chibuzo shut the room at 01:30. The new order ran exactly as written: lab results back at 02:50, the paper round covering the 30 minutes before, as rehearsed. But every result the lab sent from 02:50 showed "patient not found" on the ward screens until 04:50. The doctors went back to paper for two more hours.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did lab results say "patient not found" until 04:50, and what should the plan change?

keyIdeas.idea: Lab results depend on admissions: each result is filed against the patient's admission record, which came back at 04:50
Restore admissions with or before lab results, as one group
The impact analysis must list what each process needs, and a restore rehearsal with real systems would have caught it

coldCase.model: The lab system depends on admissions: every result is filed against the patient's admission record, and the admissions system was restored third, at 04:50. Until then the lab had results with nobody to attach them to. Restore admissions together with lab results, as one group: both first, or admissions just before the lab, with the lab's paper round covering the longer gap. Then fix the impact analysis so it lists what each process needs, not only how fast it hurts, and map the dependencies between systems. A tabletop talks through the order; only a restore test with the real systems, such as a functional exercise at the second site, shows that one system can't work without another.
